units.title: Gross Anatomy: Lobes, Oblique/Horizontal Fissures, Lower-Lobe Auscultation, Azygos Fissure 'Tadpole' & Phantom Tumor
units.sec: Gross Anatomy: Lobes, Oblique/Horizontal Fissures, Lower-Lobe Auscultation, Azygos Fissure 'Tadpole' & Phantom Tumor
units.guide:
Lobes (p185): right has 3 (RUL, RML, RLL), left has 2 (LUL, LLL); the oblique/major fissure is bilateral and the horizontal/minor fissure is right-sided. The lower lobe is not seen on a normal film because of its posterior position, needs a lateral film or CT, and is auscultated at the infrascapular and infraaxillary areas.
Fissures are depressions on the lung surface reaching the hila; type 3 is the azygos fissure, giving a tadpole appearance whose head is the azygos vein, present in 1–2% of people.
Phantom tumor/pseudotumor: fluid in the horizontal fissure, from heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, resolving with diuretics.

units.title: Phantom Tumor Resolution Films, Hilar Structures & Relations, Causes of Hilar Enlargement & Weibel's 23 Generations
units.sec: Phantom Tumor Resolution Films, Hilar Structures & Relations, Causes of Hilar Enlargement & Weibel's 23 Generations
units.guide:
Radiograph series (p186): 'Phantom tumor' → 'After 2 weeks of therapy' → 'After 4 weeks of therapy'. Hilar structures: pulmonary artery (PA), pulmonary vein (PV), bronchus, lymphatics; the PA lies anterior to the bronchus on the right and above the bronchus on the left.
Hilar enlargement: hilar lymphadenopathy (TB, sarcoidosis) and PA dilatation are bracketed 'more common'; a mediastinal mass and a mass in the bronchus complete the list.
Weibel generations total 23: conducting zone 0–16 (trachea 0 to terminal bronchioles 16) equals the anatomical dead space, 'air in the conducting zone (150 ml)'; transitional and respiratory zones 17–23 run from respiratory bronchioles through alveolar ducts (20–22) to alveolar sacs (23), bracketed as the site of gas exchange (acinus).

units.title: Bronchi Types, Right vs Left Bronchus Dimensions, Foreign-Body Predilection, Calibre/Area Change, Secondary Pulmonary Lobule & BPS Definition
units.sec: Bronchi Types, Right vs Left Bronchus Dimensions, Foreign-Body Predilection, Calibre/Area Change, Secondary Pulmonary Lobule & BPS Definition
units.guide:
Bronchi (p187) are primary/principal/main, secondary/lobar and tertiary/segmental. Right bronchus: wider (1.5 cm), shorter, steeper, 2 cm, 45° to the carina (carina at T4/5); left: narrower (1.3 cm), longer, more horizontal, 5 cm. Inhaled foreign bodies lodge R > L.
From trachea to alveoli the diameter falls from 25 mm to 0.25–0.3 mm while the cross-sectional area rises from 5 cm² to 7,00,000 cm².
The secondary pulmonary lobule is the functional unit — 3–5 terminal bronchioles within connective tissue septa — with airflow through respiratory bronchioles and alveolar ducts to alveoli; the bronchopulmonary segment is the anatomical unit supplied by a tertiary/segmental bronchus and contains the intra-segmental pulmonary artery.

units.title: Bronchopulmonary Segments of Right and Left Lung (10 Each) & Position-Dependent Aspiration Segments
units.sec: Bronchopulmonary Segments of Right and Left Lung (10 Each) & Position-Dependent Aspiration Segments
units.guide:
Segment maps (p188): both lungs have 10 segments. Right upper lobe = apical (1), posterior (2), anterior (3); middle lobe = lateral (4), medial (5); left upper lobe = apicoposterior (1, 2) and anterior (3), with the lingula as superior (4) and inferior (5) lingular. Right lower lobe = superior (6), posterior basal (7), medial basal (8), lateral basal (9), anterior basal (10).
Aspiration depends on posture: supine the posterior segment of the right upper lobe exceeds the superior segment of the right lower lobe; standing, the basal segment of the left lower lobe is involved, with R > L.

units.title: Acinus Parts, Centriacinar (Smokers) vs Panacinar (α1-Antitrypsin) Emphysema & Basal/Goblet Cells of Conducting Airways
units.sec: Acinus Parts, Centriacinar (Smokers) vs Panacinar (α1-Antitrypsin) Emphysema & Basal/Goblet Cells of Conducting Airways
units.guide:
Acinus parts (p188): respiratory bronchiole, alveolar duct and alveolus. Clinical significance: normal acinus, centriacinar emphysema (smokers) and panacinar emphysema (α-1 antitrypsin deficiency).
Cells in conducting airways begin with basal cells (stem/progenitor cells during lung injury) and goblet cells (secrete mucus).

units.title: Club (Clara) Cells, CGRP, Kulchitzky Cells, Cartilage/Smooth Muscle/Goblet Table, Epithelial Zonation & Airway Mediators
units.sec: Club (Clara) Cells, CGRP, Kulchitzky Cells, Cartilage/Smooth Muscle/Goblet Table, Epithelial Zonation & Airway Mediators
units.guide:
Club/Clara cells (p189) are non-ciliated cuboidal epithelial cells of terminal bronchioles that detoxify xenobiotics and act as progenitors for bronchiolar cells. CGRP = calcitonin gene-related peptide, a major neurotransmitter in migraine. Kulchitzky cells hold dense-core vesicles with serotonin, calcitonin and CGRP.
Structural table: cartilage + / + / –; smooth muscle – / + / + (maximal in terminal bronchiole); goblet cells – / + / – across trachea, bronchi and bronchioles. Trachea has hyaline cartilage and a glandular plus pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelial layer; bronchus epithelium is pseudostratified ciliated columnar above, ciliated simple cuboidal in the middle and simple cuboidal below; bronchiole is simple cuboidal with no mucus glands, occasional goblet cells, neuroendocrine cells clustered as neuroepithelial bodies, and Clara cells.
Mediators: leukotriene is the most potent constrictor; VIP the most potent dilator, a NANC peptide; cholinergics constrict with the methacholine challenge used to assess hyperresponsiveness; anticholinergics (ipratropium, tiotropium) dilate and are used in asthma.

units.title: Role of Cilia, Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia/Kartagener Triad, Nasal Nitric Oxide Gold Standard & Cystic Fibrosis (F508, Ivacaftor)
units.sec: Role of Cilia, Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia/Kartagener Triad, Nasal Nitric Oxide Gold Standard & Cystic Fibrosis (F508, Ivacaftor)
units.guide:
Cilia (p190) are present up to the terminal bronchiole and absent in the respiratory zone; the mucociliary escalator beats towards the nasopharynx. Immotile cilia syndrome/primary ciliary dyskinesia is autosomal recessive with a defective dynein arm, median presentation at 5 years, recurrent sinusitis and otitis media, and neonatal respiratory distress.
Kartagener's syndrome is the triad plus male infertility; cilia are needed for rotation of body organs, so their failure produces situs inversus — the triad triangle of situs inversus, sinusitis and bronchiectasis. Gold-standard investigation is nasal nitric oxide, which is always low.
Cystic fibrosis is autosomal recessive with CFTR (F508) mutation on chromosome 7q and a chloride defect: thick secretions with normal cilia affecting bronchi, biliary tract, intestine and reproductive system; ivacaftor is a chloride channel opener.

units.title: Airway Resistance: Poiseuille/Ohm Laws, Generation 5–7 Resistance Peak, Reynolds Number Flow Table
units.sec: Airway Resistance: Poiseuille/Ohm Laws, Generation 5–7 Resistance Peak, Reynolds Number Flow Table
units.guide:
From trachea to alveoli (p191) diameter, velocity and turbulence fall while total cross-sectional area rises. Ohm's law Q = ΔP/R and Poiseuille's law R = 8ηL/πr⁴, so flow ∝ 1/R and R ∝ 1/r⁴; maximal radius gives least resistance and maximal flow — hence turbulence in the trachea and laminar flow in alveoli.
Maximum resistance is at generations 5, 6 and 7 (bronchi > terminal bronchioles) because the parallel arrangement of small airways gives a maximal cross-sectional area and low resistance.
Reynolds number is proportional to velocity; >4000 is turbulent flow (trachea, bronchi), 4000–2000 transitional (respiratory bronchioles) and <2000 laminar (alveolar duct, alveoli).

units.title: Alveolar Type I vs Type II Cells, Bleomycin Effect, Surfactant Function/Components/Synthesis & GM-CSF
units.sec: Alveolar Type I vs Type II Cells, Bleomycin Effect, Surfactant Function/Components/Synthesis & GM-CSF
units.guide:
Alveolar cells (p192) are the pulmonary alveolar macrophage and the type I/II pneumocytes. Type I is 95%, a non-dividing flat squamous cell, prone to oxidative damage and injured by bleomycin, marked by aquaporin-5, caveolin-1 and carboxypeptidase m. Type II is 5%, cuboidal, repairs after injury and makes surfactant, becomes hyperplastic with bleomycin, and is marked by surfactant proteins A–D.
Notes: substance P is a bronchoconstrictor; DPPC = dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine; bronchoconstriction peaks at 6 am and bronchodilatation at 6 pm; beractant is used in hyaline membrane disease/fetal respiratory distress syndrome.
Surfactant lowers surface tension, preventing fluid accumulation (pulmonary edema) and raising compliance. Lamellar bodies in type 2 pneumocytes store and produce it; steroids (used for HMD) and thyroid hormone raise production while insulin lowers it. Lipoprotein is the major component with lecithin (DPPC) > sphingomyelin, plus proteins A–D (A and D in innate immunity); GM-CSF clears excess surfactant and its antibodies cause pulmonary alveolar proteinosis.
